query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of interstitial oxygen (around 2 at%) into the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will form ordered oxygen complexes that enhance dislocation pinning and phase boundary stability, thereby improving both strength–ductility balance and high-temperature performance (creep and corrosion resistance).
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure prepared by conventional casting, without additional controlled interstitial oxygen content.
generation.intervention: Add a controlled ~2 at% oxygen during alloy processing (e.g., by adjusting the melting atmosphere or intentional doping) to form strengthening interstitial oxygen complexes.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be processed under controlled ambient conditions that allow precise oxygen incorporation, followed by standard heat treatments. Mechanical and corrosion tests should be conducted at both room temperature and elevated operating temperatures (up to 700°C) to mimic service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered interstitial oxygen complexes within the lattice and at phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The oxygen interstitials are expected to create ordered complexes that act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby increasing yield strength and mitigating creep. Additionally, these complexes can help stabilize phase boundaries and reduce sites for corrosion initiation, contributing to improved long-term high-temperature stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped alloy is predicted to show a measurable increase in yield strength, enhanced ductility balance, and improved resistance to high-temperature creep and corrosion compared to the baseline alloy processed without controlled oxygen addition.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, which already shows a promising but insufficient combination of strength and ductility for demanding applications.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected within a narrow oxygen addition window (~1–3 at%). Exceeding this range may lead to embrittlement or undesirable second phase formation. The improvement may also depend on the specific processing conditions, cooling rates, and subsequent heat treatments.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how the long-term stability of the ordered oxygen complexes will evolve under extended high-temperature service and cyclic loading, and whether any competing phase segregation might offset the strengthening benefits over time.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples: one using standard processing (control) and the other with a controlled incorporation of ~2 at% oxygen. Subject both sets to identical heat treatment and aging protocols. Conduct mechanical testing (tensile, creep at elevated temperatures) and corrosion testing (electrochemical measurements) at room temperature and up to 700°C.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Creep rate under sustained load at elevated temperature
Electrochemical corrosion rates in a simulated aggressive environment
Microstructural analysis (using TEM/atom probe tomography) to detect the formation and stability of ordered oxygen complexes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both mechanical performance (strength–ductility and creep resistance) and corrosion resistance compared to the control samples, or if long-term aging leads to deleterious phase segregation and embrittlement, then the hypothesis that controlled interstitial oxygen addition improves practical performance will be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
